docs.node.component: A **Node** is the base of everything: an opaque `id` and a place among other nodes.
It is not abstract and not a stub — a bare node is a valid node. Everything else is an
atom: a composable interface with its own fields, methods and events. There is no kind,
no base class and no `isElement()`: behaviour asks for the atom it needs, never for a
category.
```ts
import { node, mount } from "game-kit"
const root = node("table")        // a name and a place in the tree — nothing else
mount(document.querySelector("#app"), root)   // empty on screen, and that is correct
`mount` is the HOST: it takes a DOM element to live in, creates the `view` inside it (the
`HTMLCanvasElement` — never called `canvas` in code), measures the viewport and watches it
for resizes. Nodes know units; the host is the only thing here that knows pixels.
**A node is NAMED — it does not name itself.** The id is an input, because the same node is
read from more than one place: another player's device, a save reopened tomorrow, a live
mock watching the same canvas. A counter hidden inside `node()` would be unique in one tab
and nowhere else, and the failure it makes is the quiet kind — a move arrives and lands on
a DIFFERENT existing node instead of a missing one.
So a name comes from one of two places, both outside the node: **the spec**, for authored
nodes (`table`, `hand`, `discard` — data, identical for everyone who loads that board), and
**the world's orchestrator**, for nodes born during play — the room, the save, or
`localIds()` when the instance answers to nobody.
Either way the id is **opaque**: nothing parses it, splits it, or compares it to a literal.
A speaking name is for the human reading the tree.
**Not everything is a node.** A slot is an address, a spreading gap is a layout phantom,
a shadow is a layer, a camera is a way of looking — none of them has an `id`. A
transaction is not a node either and not a descendant of one: asking it for its `z` or
its shadow is meaningless. It stands above nodes and uses them.
docs.node.bare: One node in a vacuum. The stage is empty — not unfinished: no atom here paints, so there
is nothing to draw. **The scene is the node tree**, in the block under the canvas here
and in the panel next to Controls in story mode.
The inspector reports `atoms: none — an id and a place, and that is valid`. That line is
the whole point of this story: emptiness is a legal state of the model, not a gap in it.
docs.root.component: There is no separate storage entity. Every node hangs off a root, so **the root IS the
storage** — an ordinary node. Nothing stands above the roots, so no word was needed for
'the thing that holds them'.
**A root is a node that nobody placed.** It has no owner, and it has no size of its own:
its extent comes from its content. That is also why a root can never become someone's
child — it would stop being a root.
```ts
import { node, add, byId } from "game-kit"
const root = node("table")
add(root, node("hand"))       // a child; the root is still the only thing nobody placed
byId(root, "hand")           // a DERIVED index over the tree, never a second store
**One name per tree.** Adding a second `hand` throws, and so does adding a subtree that
carries a taken name anywhere inside it. Replacing the older node instead would be worse
than the error: a picture that still looks right, built on an identity that was lost.
Two separate trees may each hold a `hand` — they only have to agree inside one tree.
**Two roots, one difference.** The camera transforms `CanvasRoot` and does not touch
`HudRoot`. That is the anchor law in full — there is no `anchor` field, belonging to a
root IS the answer. 'Canvas' is that camera-driven root, not a separate storage.
**Pixels live in the host.** A node knows units. The host owns the `view` (the
`HTMLCanvasElement` — never called `canvas` in code), its size and the resize observer,
and computes the HUD etalon as a fraction of the viewport.
docs.root.withChildren: A root holding two children — `table`, and under it `hand` and `discard`. Read the tree top
down: only the first entry is marked `root, nobody places it`; the other two have an owner,
and that is the entire difference between a root and everything else.
Those three names come from the SPEC, not from a generator. Every device loading this board
reads the same three, which is what lets them agree on which node a move is about.
Nothing here needed a `Container` atom. Parent and child are BASE: a place in the tree
has two directions, and one without the other is meaningless. `Container` will add HOW
children are arranged — that they exist at all is not its business.
docs.root.alone: The same node as `Node → Bare`, seen from the other side: nobody placed it, so it is a
root. Being a root is not a type or a flag — it is the absence of an owner. Detach a
child from its parent and it becomes a root too, on the spot.
docs.bounded.component: **Bounded** is the box — the first atom that divides the model, and it divides it three
ways at once: a finger needs a hit area, a shadow needs a silhouette, an owner's layout
needs somewhere to put the child. All three are the same shape, which is why they are one
atom rather than three fields scattered about.
```ts
import { node, Bounded, footprint } from "game-kit"
const card = node("card", Bounded())                 // rect 1×1, in UNITS, never pixels
footprint(card)   // { kind: "rect", w: 1, h: 1 }
footprint(node("ghost"))   // undefined — no box at all, which is not a zero box
The default is a **1×1 rect — a square**, and that has to be said out loud rather than left
to be inferred. Read as a claim about cards it would say "elements are square", which is
not what a plainest-possible default means.
**It paints NOT ONE PIXEL.** There is no fill here, no border, no radius — look at the
inspector and the only fields are `size` and `bounds`. A look belongs to a `surface`
record (see `Surfaced`), and no "bounds outline" exists in the model at all: the box is
visible to the inspector and to a debug layer, and to nothing else.
**`bounds` is about ITSELF, and that is all.** One field may not mean two things: it
overrides this instance's own `size` and does not mean "keep the content inside". Children
are placed by a LAYOUT, and out of a row or a grid a child cannot walk by construction.
Sizes are in **units**. The host is the only thing that knows what a unit is worth on
screen, and a size that arrived in pixels would be a different size on every phone.
docs.bounded.box: One node, one box, and the stage is still empty — the same emptiness as `Node → Bare`, now
for a different reason. There is a place taken and nothing to show for it.
The inspector is where the difference lives: `Bounded.size` reads `{"kind":"rect","w":1,
"h":1}` and `Bounded.bounds` reads `—`. An absent optional field is shown as absent rather
than filled in with a plausible value.
docs.surfaced.component: **Surfaced** is the atom that draws. Everything else in the model merely exists.
Its requirement is the reason requirements may be **alternatives** at all. A surface needs
an AREA, and an area has two sources: an own box (`Bounded`) or the extent of the content
(`Container`). Demanding `Bounded` would outlaw the tabletop — the one node the whole table
is built on, which has something to paint and no footprint of its own.
```ts
import { node, Bounded, Surfaced, registerSurface } from "game-kit"
registerSurface("plate", { fill: "panelBg", border: "accent", borderWidth: 0.03 })
const card = node("card", Bounded(), Surfaced({ surface: "plate" }))
registerSurface("plate", { fill: "panelBg" })   // border gone, everywhere, at once
**`surface` is a REFERENCE, not a bag of colours on the node.** Re-register the record and
every card loses its border in one step while not one box moves a unit — that separation is
what the story is for, and inline fields could not demonstrate it. It also keeps the wire
honest: `"plate"` is the same short string on every client, whereas a palette copied into
each message is state two clients may legitimately disagree about, and a saved game would
reopen in last year's colours.
**An unregistered name is skipped, not thrown.** A dangling reference is a content mistake,
and taking the whole scene down over one would hide every node that was perfectly fine.
**`fit` and `align` come FROM THE OWNER**, so they are absent by default rather than
pre-filled with `contain`. A field carrying its default on every node is a field that is
always set — and then nothing is ever inherited from anywhere. The fallback is applied when
the value is resolved, not when the node is built.
docs.surfaced.plate: The same square as `Bounded → Box`, one atom later, and now it can be seen. Nothing about
the box changed: the border and the radius arrived from the `plate` record, and the model
Read the inspector next to it: `Surfaced.surface` says `plate`, while `Surfaced.fit` and
`Surfaced.align` say `—`. The look is NAMED here and described elsewhere.
docs.surfaced.table: A surface on a node with **no box of its own**. The area comes from what the node HOLDS,
which is the whole reason the requirement is an alternative rather than `Bounded`.
This is the tabletop, and it is an ordinary node — not a special "canvas" entity. Take the
children away and there is nothing left to paint on: the extent of nothing is zero, not
docs.transformable.component: **Transformable** is the node's own pose: where it sits, and how high it stands. It lives
on a bare `Node` and needs no box — a node can be somewhere without occupying anything, and
the tabletop is exactly such a node.
Its two fields are deliberately in **different inheritance classes**, and that is the whole
at   own      // a position is about THIS node; inside a container the layout resolves it
z    addsUp   // lift a stack and everything in it rises with it
`z` **cannot be cancelled by a child, only added to** — which is what anyone expects from
picking up a pack of cards. The apparent contradiction with "a stack's thickness is layout,
not `z`" dissolves once the classes are read: **a layout may write `at` and may not write
`z`**, and here that is not a convention but a type — a layout returns points, and a point
has no `z` to write. A card inside a resting stack does not rise, because thickness is an
Nothing resolved is stored on the node or sent over the wire. `z` is summed along the chain
**at apply time**, so a node that changes owner mid-animation gets the new answer. In
client1 a base frozen when a flight began broke the fan's order three times over.

docs.container.component: **Container is not "it has children"** — it is HOW they are arranged.
Parent and child are BASE: a root already holds children with no atom composed on it at
all. So an atom carrying only the link would carry nothing. Take the arrangement out of
The neighbouring question — "where is this node itself" — belongs to `Transformable`, and
keeping the two apart is what makes a free canvas an ORDINARY case rather than a special
import { node, add, Container, Transformable, placeChildren } from "game-kit"
const table = node("table", Container({ layout: "free" }))   // places nobody
add(table, node("card", Transformable({ at: { x: 2, y: 0 } })))
placeChildren(table).get("card")   // { x: 2, y: 0 } — the child's own pose stands
**`free` places nobody; `row` places everyone.** They are chosen to be opposites, and the
two stories differ in that one word alone.
**Spacing belongs to the RECORD, not to the container.** A gap means something in a row and
nothing in a free layout, and a field four arrangements out of five cannot use is a field
that gets misread. The same reasoning keeps `clamp` and `cast` out of the atom.
**An unknown layout places nobody** rather than throwing, for the same reason an unknown
surface is skipped: a content mistake must not take the scene down with it.
docs.container.free: Three plates, each with a pose of its own, under a layout that declines to place them. This
is the "canvas you can put things anywhere on" — and it is not a mode or a second kind of
container. It is the CHEAPEST layout record there is, one that returns nothing for every
Compare with `Row`: the tree is identical, down to the poses. Only the layout's name differs.

that places, places: what the children asked for is overridden, not added to.
